name: Recursion Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
subcategory: AI-driven drug discovery ('TechBio'), automated phenomics data factory, clinical-stage
origin_detail: Founded 5 Nov 2013 in Salt Lake City, Utah; co-founder Chris Gibson was CEO until 31 Dec 2025. A University of Utah spin-out origin is often reported but was not confirmed in any fetched source, so origin is null. Acquired UK-listed Exscientia on 20 Nov 2024.
flagship_projects: Recursion OS / phenomics platform (>2M experiments per week)
RxRx open datasets (RxRx1, RxRx2, RxRx19a/b, RxRx3, RxRx3-core)
Boltz-2 (MIT-licensed structure/affinity model listed on rxrx.ai)
openness_notes: The platform, the proprietary dataset and the pipeline are closed. Since 2019 Recursion has released curated samples: RxRx1 (June 2019, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, 'less than 1% of its weekly data generation'), with a NeurIPS/Kaggle competition. RxRx3-core followed (2025, Hugging Face, 222,601 wells; licence not shown on the pages fetched). OpenPhenom (ViT-S/16 MAE trained on RxRx3 plus public JUMP-CP data) is under a 'Non-Commercial End User License Agreement'. Boltz-2 is listed on rxrx.ai and tagged MIT on Hugging Face. rxrx.ai says its public datasets 'represent less than 1% of Recursion's full, proprietary dataset.' These are peripheral, mostly non-commercial releases around a closed core: level 1.

10 Jun 2025: ~20% workforce reduction (~$11M charges) under a 'streamlined operating strategy' and post-integration transitions; runway guided into Q4 2027; cash burn guided below $390M for 2026
FY2025: revenue $74.7M, net loss $644.8M (TTM to 30 Sep 2026: revenue $68.2M, net loss $475.7M)
FY2025 10-K: REC-2282, REC-994 and REC-3964 discontinued or seeking partners
1 Jan 2026: co-founder Chris Gibson stepped down as CEO (became Chair); Najat Khan became CEO
Market cap: ~$2.92B at the 2021 IPO, $2.89B at end-2021, $1.46B end-2022, $2.67B end-2024, $1.66B on 23 Nov 2026
robustness: Public and well partnered: more than $500M in cumulative upfront and milestone payments, including Roche/Genentech ($213M) and Sanofi ($134M), with Bayer and Merck KGaA also partners. It runs an NVIDIA-built supercomputer (BioHive-2) and automated labs doing over 2M experiments a week. Cash burn is heavy and value depends on clinical readouts for five wholly owned clinical programs. The proprietary phenomics dataset is the core asset, and the open releases are sized so as not to give it away.
physical_science_relevance: Low to moderate. The work is biology and drug discovery, not physical science. But Recursion is the leading example of an industrialized, closed-loop automated-lab 'data factory' feeding ML models, the architecture that materials-focused entrants (Lila, Periodic Labs) now pitch. Its RxRx strategy, releasing a non-commercial sample of under 1% of its data as benchmarks, is a template others copy. OpenPhenom also shows reliance on public consortium data (JUMP-CP) alongside proprietary data.
openness_effect_assessment: Recursion uses openness as a benchmark, community and recruiting tool around a closed core. It has released datasets since 2019 and models later, mostly under non-commercial terms, explicitly representing under 1% of its data. That seeded ML benchmarks and competitions, but its value is the proprietary dataset and pipeline. Openness did not shield it from the 2024-2026 TechBio downturn (merger, 20% layoffs, founder-CEO transition, market cap below its IPO level).
key_takeaway: Recursion is the public-market test of the 'automated lab plus AI' thesis. After 13 years and the Exscientia merger it has about $75M in revenue, a net loss of roughly $645M (2025) and a $1.66B market cap, below its 2021 IPO level. Its open-science activity (RxRx, OpenPhenom, Boltz-2) is real but deliberately peripheral: curated, mostly non-commercial releases of under 1% of its data, sometimes trained on public consortium data, while the data that matter stay proprietary. It anticipates the 'open papers and benchmarks, closed data' pattern of the 2025-2026 AI-for-science labs.
